title: Ἑταίρων λύσις
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Circe sees Odysseus sitting grief-stricken over the food and asks why he will not eat. He answers that no man of any feeling could taste food before he has seen his companions freed. She goes out, opens the sty and smears each of the beasts with another drug; the bristles fall away, and they become men again, younger and fairer than before, and weep at the sight of him. At her bidding Odysseus goes down to the ship and finds the crew weeping there; they greet him as gladly as if he had reached Ithaca. He tells them to haul the ship up and follow him to Circe's hall, but Eurylochus alone tries to hold them back, speaking of the Cyclops and blaming Odysseus for what happened there. Odysseus thinks of striking off his head, but the others restrain him, and Eurylochus follows after all, in fear of his rebuke. In the hall the restored men have been bathed and clothed and are feasting; Circe tells them to eat and drink until their spirits come back, and they stay on feasting for a year, until the crew call Odysseus out and remind him of home.

sentences.t:
Κίρκη δ’ ὡς ἐνόησεν ἔμ’ ἥμενον οὐδ’ ἐπὶ σίτῳ
χεῖρας ἰάλλοντα, κρατερὸν δέ με πένθος ἔχοντα,
ἄγχι παρισταμένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
Kirkē d’ hōs enoēsen em’ hēmenon oud’ epi sitōi
cheiras iallonta, krateron de me penthos echonta,
anchi paristamenē epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And Circe, when she noticed me sitting, and not upon food
hands putting forth, and strong grief holding me,
close beside me standing, winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: When Circe noticed me sitting there, not putting my hands to the food, and gripped by strong grief, she came and stood close beside me and spoke winged words:
sentences.n: Odysseus, still telling his tale, describes how Circe notices that he will not eat. ὡς ἐνόησεν is ‘when she noticed’, with two accusative participles: ἔμ’ ἥμενον ‘me sitting’ (ἧμαι) and χεῖρας ἰάλλοντα ‘putting out my hands’ (ἰάλλω ‘send, put forth’); the third, ἔχοντα, agrees with με and has κρατερὸν πένθος ‘strong grief’ as its object. ἄγχι παρισταμένη is ‘standing beside, near’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula ‘spoke winged words’; the edition ends the line with a raised point, and the speech itself begins in the next unit. The Greek prints no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
τίφθ’ οὕτως, Ὀδυσεῦ, κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζεαι ἶσος ἀναύδῳ,
θυμὸν ἔδων, βρώμης δ’ οὐχ ἅπτεαι οὐδὲ ποτῆτος;
sentences.tr:
tiphth’ houtōs, Odyseu, kat’ ar’ hezeai isos anaudōi,
thymon edōn, brōmēs d’ ouch hapteai oude potētos;
sentences.l:
‘Why so, Odysseus, do you sit, like to a speechless one,
heart eating, and of food you do not touch, nor of drink?
sentences.i: ‘Why do you sit like this, Odysseus, like a man who cannot speak, eating your heart out, and touch neither food nor drink?
sentences.n: Circe speaks, in the second person. τίφθ’ is τίπτε (= τί ποτε) ‘why’, elided before the rough breathing of οὕτως, which turns πτ into φθ. ἕζεαι is the uncontracted second person of ἕζομαι ‘sit’ (= ἕζῃ), and κατ’ … ἕζεαι is tmesis, ‘you sit down’. ἶσος ἀναύδῳ is ‘equal to a speechless one’, ἄναυδος being ‘without voice’. θυμὸν ἔδων ‘eating the heart’ is an idiom for brooding grief. ἅπτεαι (= ἅπτῃ) takes the genitive, βρώμης … ποτῆτος ‘of food … of drink’.

sentences.t: ἦ τινά που δόλον ἄλλον ὀίεαι·
sentences.tr: ē tina pou dolon allon oieai·
sentences.l: Surely some other trick, I suppose, you suspect;
sentences.i: Surely you suspect some other trick;
sentences.n: ἦ with a circumflex is ‘truly, surely’ (ἢ ‘or’ is another word); some readers take it as the opener of a question, ‘can it be that …?’, and the edition's raised point does not decide. που softens the guess to ‘I suppose’. ὀίεαι is the uncontracted second person of ὀίομαι ‘think, suspect’ (= οἴῃ). δόλον ἄλλον is ‘another trick’, one beyond the trick she has already played on his men.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
δειδίμεν·
sentences.tr:
oude ti se chrē
deidimen·
sentences.l:
and not at all do you need
to fear;
sentences.i: and you have no need at all to fear;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τί σε χρή is ‘and there is no need for you’: χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the accusative of the person and an infinitive. δειδίμεν is the perfect infinitive of δείδω ‘fear’, with present sense, in the short ending -μεν (= δεδιέναι). The unit ends at the raised point after the infinitive, and the reason follows.

sentences.t: ἤδη γάρ τοι ἀπώμοσα καρτερὸν ὅρκον.
sentences.tr: ēdē gar toi apōmosa karteron horkon.
sentences.l: for already to you I have sworn a strong oath.’
sentences.i: for I have already sworn you a strong oath.’
sentences.n: ἀπώμοσα is the aorist of ἀπόμνυμι ‘swear solemnly’, and τοι is the enclitic σοι ‘to you’. καρτερός is a by-form of κρατερός ‘strong’. The oath is the one Circe took, at Odysseus' demand, before he would go to her bed; she gives it here as the proof that she means no further harm.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar egō min ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατο, here elided, is ‘so she spoke’. αὐτάρ is the epic ‘but, and’. ἀμειβόμενος is ‘answering’ (ἀμείβομαι), and προσέειπον is ‘I addressed’, the first person of the aorist whose third person is προσέειπε; μιν is the pronoun ‘her’. The edition ends with a raised point, and Odysseus' reply begins in the next unit.

sentences.l:
‘O Circe, for what man, who might be one with a sense of what is fitting,
before he would bring himself to taste of food and of drink,
before he had freed his companions and seen them with his eyes?
sentences.i: ‘Circe, what man with any sense of what is fitting could bring himself to taste food and drink before he had freed his companions and seen them with his own eyes?
sentences.n: Odysseus answers; the Greek prints no quotation marks. τίς γάρ … is a rhetorical ‘for what man …?’, with κεν and the optative τλαίη ‘would bring himself’ (τλάω ‘endure, dare’). ἐναίσιμος is built on αἶσα ‘portion, due’, so a man who keeps to what is due and fitting; it is a relative clause, ὃς … εἴη. πάσσασθαι is ‘to taste’ with the genitive ἐδητύος … ποτῆτος ‘food … drink’. The two πρίν answer each other (‘would dare … before …’), and the second takes the infinitives λύσασθ’ ‘to free (his own)’ and ἰδέσθαι ‘to see’. ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is ‘with the eyes’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰ δὴ πρόφρασσα πιεῖν φαγέμεν τε κελεύεις,
λῦσον, ἵν’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδω ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
all’ ei dē prophrassa piein phagemen te keleueis,
lyson, hin’ ophthalmoisin idō eriēras hetairous.
sentences.l:
But if indeed, ready-minded, to drink and to eat you bid me,
release them, that with my eyes I may see my trusty companions.’
sentences.i: But if you truly bid me, with a ready mind, to drink and eat, free them, so that I may see my trusty companions with my own eyes.’
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ εἰ δή is ‘but if indeed’. πρόφρασσα is the epic feminine of πρόφρων ‘with a ready mind’, agreeing with Circe, so the readiness is hers. πιεῖν and φαγέμεν are aorist infinitives, the second in -έμεν. λῦσον is the aorist imperative of λύω ‘loose, release’; ἵν’ … ἴδω is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive. ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους is ‘trusty companions’; the sense of ἐρίηρος is not fully known, and the first element is probably the intensive ἐρι-.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, Κίρκη δὲ διὲκ μεγάροιο βεβήκει
ῥάβδον ἔχουσ’ ἐν χειρί, θύρας δ’ ἀνέῳξε συφειοῦ,
ἐκ δ’ ἔλασεν σιάλοισιν ἐοικότας ἐννεώροισιν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephamēn, Kirkē de diek megaroio bebēkei
rhabdon echous’ en cheiri, thyras d’ aneōixe sypheiou,
ek d’ elasen sialoisin eoikotas enneōroisin.
sentences.l:
So I spoke, and Circe out through the hall had gone,
a wand holding in her hand, and the doors she opened of the sty,
and drove out, like to fat hogs, nine-year-olds.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and Circe went out through the hall with her wand in her hand, opened the doors of the sty, and drove out creatures that looked like fat nine-year-old hogs.
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’ (imperfect of φημί). βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone’, with διέκ ‘out through’ and the genitive μεγάροιο. ῥάβδον ἔχουσ’ is ‘holding a wand’, and ἀνέῳξε (ἀνοίγνυμι) ‘opened’. ἐκ … ἔλασεν is tmesis, ‘drove out’. The object is left to be understood: the men in pigs' shapes. σίαλος is a fat hog, and ἐννεώροισιν ‘nine-year-old’ is an adjective agreeing with it; the dative follows ἐοικότας ‘like’.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἔστησαν ἐναντίοι, ἡ δὲ δι’ αὐτῶν
ἐρχομένη προσάλειφεν ἑκάστῳ φάρμακον ἄλλο.
sentences.tr:
hoi men epeit’ estēsan enantioi, hē de di’ autōn
erchomenē prosaleiphen hekastōi pharmakon allo.
sentences.l:
They then stood opposite, and she through the midst of them
going smeared on each another drug.
sentences.i: They then stood facing her, and she went through the midst of them and smeared another drug on each.
sentences.n: οἱ μέν ‘they’ are the transformed men, and ἐναντίοι is ‘opposite, facing (her)’. δι’ αὐτῶν is ‘through the midst of them’. προσάλειφεν is the imperfect of προσαλείφω ‘smear on’, with ἑκάστῳ ‘on each one’. ἄλλο is ‘another, a different’ drug: the one that undoes the first. The imperfect shows her going from man to man.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἐκ μὲν μελέων τρίχες ἔρρεον, ἃς πρὶν ἔφυσε
φάρμακον οὐλόμενον, τό σφιν πόρε πότνια Κίρκη·
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ ek men meleōn triches erreon, has prin ephyse
pharmakon oulomenon, to sphin pore potnia Kirkē·
sentences.l:
And from their limbs the bristles flowed away, which before had grown
the ruinous drug, which to them had given the lady Circe;
sentences.i: And the bristles dropped away from their limbs, the bristles that the ruinous drug had grown on them, the drug that the lady Circe had given them;
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἔρρεον is tmesis, ‘flowed off, fell away’. ἃς πρὶν ἔφυσε is ‘which before had caused to grow’: ἔφυσε is the transitive aorist of φύω, with φάρμακον οὐλόμενον ‘the ruinous drug’ as its subject. οὐλόμενος is the participle of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’ in the middle, ‘destructive, accursed’; it is another word than ὀλοός. πόρε ‘gave’ is unaugmented, σφιν the enclitic dative ‘to them’, and πότνια Κίρκη ‘the lady Circe’.

sentences.t:
ἄνδρες δ’ ἂψ ἐγένοντο νεώτεροι ἢ πάρος ἦσαν,
καὶ πολὺ καλλίονες καὶ μείζονες εἰσοράασθαι.
sentences.tr:
andres d’ aps egenonto neōteroi ē paros ēsan,
kai poly kalliones kai meizones eisoraasthai.
sentences.l:
and men again they became, younger than before they were,
and much fairer and taller to look upon.
sentences.i: and they became men again, younger than they had been before, and much fairer and taller to look at.
sentences.n: ἄψ ‘back, again’ goes with ἐγένοντο. νεώτεροι ἢ πάρος ἦσαν is ‘younger than before they were’: ἢ ‘than’ follows the comparative. καλλίονες and μείζονες are the comparatives of καλός ‘fair’ and μέγας ‘great, tall’. εἰσοράασθαι is the uncontracted passive infinitive of εἰσοράω (Attic εἰσορᾶσθαι), here ‘to be looked at’, an infinitive of respect: ‘to look upon’.

sentences.t: ἔγνωσαν δέ μ’ ἐκεῖνοι ἔφυν τ’ ἐν χερσὶν ἕκαστος.
sentences.tr: egnōsan de m’ ekeinoi ephyn t’ en chersin hekastos.
sentences.l: And they knew me, those men, and took-firm-hold in my hands, each one.
sentences.i: Those men knew me, and each of them took firm hold of my hands.
sentences.n: ἔγνωσαν is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’, and ἐκεῖνοι ‘those men’ points back to the restored crew. ἐν … ἔφυν is tmesis: ἔφυν is the intransitive aorist of φύω ‘grow’, so ‘grew into’, idiomatically ‘took firm hold of’; the verb is the same one as in the singular idiom ‘took him by the hand’, here with the plural χερσίν ‘in my hands’ and ἕκαστος ‘each one’ in apposition to the subject.

sentences.t:
πᾶσιν δ’ ἱμερόεις ὑπέδυ γόος, ἀμφὶ δὲ δῶμα
σμερδαλέον κονάβιζε·
sentences.tr:
pasin d’ himeroeis hypedy goos, amphi de dōma
smerdaleon konabize·
sentences.l:
And on all a lament full of longing crept beneath, and around the house
terribly rang;
sentences.i: A lament full of longing came over them all, and the house rang terribly all around;
sentences.n: ἱμερόεις is built on ἵμερος ‘longing’ with the suffix -όεις ‘full of’: a lament that stirs the longing to weep and to be home. ὑπέδυ is the aorist of ὑποδύομαι, ‘crept under, came over’, with the dative πᾶσιν. ἀμφὶ δὲ δῶμα … κονάβιζε is ‘and all round the house resounded’: κονάβιζε is imperfect of κοναβίζω ‘ring, clatter’, from κόναβος ‘din’; σμερδαλέον, a neuter used as an adverb, is ‘terribly’. The line is cut at the raised point, mid-line.

sentences.t: θεὰ δ’ ἐλέαιρε καὶ αὐτή.
sentences.tr: thea d’ eleaire kai autē.
sentences.l: and the goddess pitied them, even herself.
sentences.i: and even the goddess herself felt pity.
sentences.n: θεά is Circe, as the ‘goddess’. ἐλέαιρε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐλεαίρω ‘pity’, and its object ‘them’ is understood. καὶ αὐτή is ‘even she herself’: pity from the one who caused the sorrow.

sentences.t: ἡ δέ μευ ἄγχι στᾶσα προσηύδα δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: hē de meu anchi stasa prosēuda dia theaōn·
sentences.l: And she, close to me having stood, spoke to me, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: And she, heavenly even among goddesses, came and stood close beside me and spoke:
sentences.n: μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ (= μου), governed by ἄγχι ‘near’. στᾶσα is the aorist participle of ἵστημι ‘having stood’, and προσηύδα ‘spoke to’. δῖα θεάων is ‘heavenly among goddesses’: θεάων is the uncontracted genitive plural, partitive, and δῖα is Circe's epithet here as it is Calypso's at 1.14. The same line returns at 455, where it opens Circe's second speech.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
ἔρχεο νῦν ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν καὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
diogenes Laertiadē, polymēchan’ Odysseu,
ercheo nyn epi nēa thoēn kai thina thalassēs.
sentences.l:
‘Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
go now to the swift ship and the shore of the sea.
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, go now to the swift ship and the shore of the sea.
sentences.n: Circe speaks. Λαερτιάδη is the vocative of the patronymic Λαερτιάδης ‘son of Laertes’, with διογενές ‘Zeus-born’ and πολυμήχαν’ (= πολυμήχανε) ‘of many devices’: the full formal address, which tells him she knows who he is. ἔρχεο is the uncontracted imperative of ἔρχομαι (= ἔρχου). θῖνα is the accusative of θίς ‘beach, shore’.
sentences.mark: Circe sends Odysseus to the ship

sentences.t:
νῆα μὲν ἂρ πάμπρωτον ἐρύσσατε ἤπειρόνδε,
κτήματα δ’ ἐν σπήεσσι πελάσσατε ὅπλα τε πάντα·
sentences.tr:
nēa men ar pamprōton eryssate ēpeironde,
ktēmata d’ en spēessi pelassate hopla te panta·
sentences.l:
The ship, then, first of all haul up onto land,
and the goods in caves bring near, and all the gear;
sentences.i: First of all haul your ship up onto the land, and lay up your goods and all your tackle in caves;
sentences.n: ἐρύσσατε is the plural imperative of ἐρύω ‘draw, haul’: the ship is dragged up the beach. ἄρ is the particle ἄρα ‘then’. πάμπρωτον is ‘first of all’, and ἤπειρόνδε ‘to the land’ has the direction suffix -δε. πελάσσατε is ‘bring near, put’; the goods and the ὅπλα ‘gear, the ship's tackle’ are to be stored in the σπήεσσι, the dative plural of σπέος ‘cave’ (σπέσσι in the other form). Circe addresses Odysseus but the plural verbs are for the whole crew.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς δ’ ἂψ ἰέναι καὶ ἄγειν ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr: autos d’ aps ienai kai agein eriēras hetairous.
sentences.l: and yourself back to go, and to bring trusty companions.’
sentences.i: then come back yourself and bring your trusty companions.’
sentences.n: ἰέναι and ἄγειν are infinitives used as commands, continuing the imperatives before them: ‘and go back yourself and bring’. αὐτός ‘yourself’ contrasts Odysseus with the crew who stay with the ship, and ἂψ ‘back’ is the same adverb as in line 395. ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους is the formula for ‘trusty companions’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γ’ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ,
βῆν δ’ ἰέναι ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν καὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, autar emoi g’ epepeitheto thymos agēnōr,
bēn d’ ienai epi nēa thoēn kai thina thalassēs.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and for my part was persuaded my manly spirit,
and I set out to go to the swift ship and the shore of the sea.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and, for my part, my proud spirit was persuaded, and I set out for the swift ship and the shore of the sea.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατο ‘so she spoke’ closes Circe's speech. ἐπεπείθετο is the imperfect middle of πείθω ‘persuade’ (middle ‘be persuaded, obey’), here with the dative ἐμοί γε ‘for me, for my part’. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is a fixed phrase: ἀγήνωρ ‘manly, proud’ (ἀγα- + ἀνήρ) is not a reproach here. βῆν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, with the infinitive ἰέναι ‘I set out to go’. The second line repeats line 402's ending.

sentences.t:
εὗρον ἔπειτ’ ἐπὶ νηὶ θοῇ ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους
οἴκτρ’ ὀλοφυρομένους, θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέοντας.
sentences.tr:
heuron epeit’ epi nēi thoēi eriēras hetairous
oiktr’ olophyromenous, thaleron kata dakry cheontas.
sentences.l:
I found then, by the swift ship, my trusty companions
pitifully lamenting, an abundant tear shedding.
sentences.i: By the swift ship I found my trusty companions, pitifully lamenting and shedding abundant tears.
sentences.n: εὗρον is the unaugmented aorist of εὑρίσκω ‘find’, and νηὶ θοῇ the dative ‘by the swift ship’. οἴκτρ’ is the neuter plural οἰκτρά of οἰκτρός ‘pitiable’ used as an adverb, ‘pitifully’. ὀλοφυρομένους is ‘lamenting’, and δάκρυ χέοντας ‘shedding a tear’, with the singular for the many. θαλερόν is ‘blooming, luxuriant’; of tears it means full, copious.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἄγραυλοι πόριες περὶ βοῦς ἀγελαίας,
ἐλθούσας ἐς κόπρον, ἐπὴν βοτάνης κορέσωνται,
πᾶσαι ἅμα σκαίρουσιν ἐναντίαι·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ an agrauloi pories peri bous agelaias,
elthousas es kopron, epēn botanēs koresōntai,
pasai hama skairousin enantiai·
sentences.i: As when calves that live in the fields all frisk together around the cows of the herd, facing them, as they come to the yard, when they have had their fill of grazing;
sentences.n: A simile: the men crowd round Odysseus as calves round their mothers. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν is ‘just as when’, and ἄγραυλοι is ‘living out in the fields’ (ἀγρός + αὐλή), of πόριες ‘calves’. βοῦς is feminine, ‘cows’, with ἀγελαίας ‘of the herd’ and ἐλθούσας ‘come’; κόπρον is the yard where the cattle are penned, and ἐπὴν … κορέσωνται is ‘after they have had their fill’ (κορέννυμι) of βοτάνης ‘grazing’. σκαίρουσιν is ‘skip, bound’, and ἐναντίαι ‘face to face’. The unit is cut at the raised point inside line 412.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἔτι σηκοὶ
ἴσχουσ’, ἀλλ’ ἁδινὸν μυκώμεναι ἀμφιθέουσι·
μητέρας·
sentences.tr:
oud’ eti sēkoi
ischous’, all’ hadinon mykōmenai amphitheousi·
mēteras·
sentences.i: and the pens can no longer hold them in, but lowing heavily they run round their mothers;
sentences.n: The simile continues. οὐδ’ ἔτι is ‘and no longer’, and σηκοί ‘pens, folds’ is the subject of ἴσχουσ’ (= ἴσχουσι ‘hold, hold back’), the calves being understood as its object. ἁδινόν is ‘thick, close-packed’ and goes with μυκώμεναι ‘lowing’ (μυκάομαι): a thick, unbroken lowing. ἀμφιθέουσι is ‘run round’ (ἀμφί + θέω), and its object μητέρας, ‘mothers’, falls at the start of the next line.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔμ’ ἐκεῖνοι ἐπεὶ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι,
δακρυόεντες ἔχυντο·
sentences.tr:
hōs em’ ekeinoi epei idon ophthalmoisi,
dakryoentes echynto·
sentences.l:
so me, those men, when they saw me with their eyes,
tearful, poured themselves forth;
sentences.i: so those men, when they saw me with their own eyes, came streaming forward in tears;
sentences.n: ὣς is the ‘so’ that answers the simile's ‘as’. ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω ‘saw’, with ὀφθαλμοῖσι ‘with the eyes’. δακρυόεντες is ‘tearful’ (δάκρυ + -όεις ‘full of’). ἔχυντο is the aorist middle of χέω ‘pour’, ‘poured themselves out, streamed’; the Greek does not name where they streamed to. The unit is cut at the raised point inside line 415.

sentences.t:
δόκησε δ’ ἄρα σφίσι θυμὸς
ὣς ἔμεν, ὡς εἰ πατρίδ’ ἱκοίατο καὶ πόλιν αὐτὴν
τρηχείης Ἰθάκης, ἵνα τ’ ἔτραφεν ἠδ’ ἐγένοντο.
sentences.tr:
dokēse d’ ara sphisi thymos
hōs emen, hōs ei patrid’ hikoiato kai polin autēn
trēcheiēs Ithakēs, hina t’ etraphen ēd’ egenonto.
sentences.l:
and it seemed to them in heart
so to be, as if to their fatherland they had come and the very town
of rough Ithaca, where they were reared and were born.
sentences.i: and in their hearts it seemed to them that they had come to their fatherland and the very town of rough Ithaca, where they had been reared and born.
sentences.n: δόκησε is an unaugmented aorist of δοκέω ‘seem’, with the dative σφίσι ‘to them’ and θυμός ‘heart’ as nominative subject (literally ‘their heart seemed so to them’, put in English as ‘in their hearts it seemed’); ὣς ἔμεν is ‘to be so’ (ἔμεν = εἶναι). ὡς εἰ … ἱκοίατο is ‘as if they had come’, the optative in -οίατο being the epic form of -οιντο (ἱκνέομαι ‘come, reach’). πόλιν αὐτήν is ‘the very town’. τρηχείης is the Ionic feminine of τρηχύς ‘rough’, the epithet of Ithaca. ἔτραφεν is the epic third plural (= ἐτράφησαν) of the passive aorist of τρέφω ‘rear’, ‘they were reared’, beside ἐγένοντο ‘they were born’.

sentences.t: καί μ’ ὀλοφυρόμενοι ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδων·
sentences.tr: kai m’ olophyromenoi epea pteroenta prosēudōn·
sentences.l: And to me, lamenting, winged words they spoke:
sentences.i: And, lamenting, they spoke winged words to me:
sentences.n: καί μ’ is καί με ‘and me’. ὀλοφυρόμενοι ‘lamenting’ is the middle participle of ὀλοφύρομαι, and προσηύδων is the plural imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. The line ends in the formula ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδων and the speech follows; it is the plural counterpart of the singular προσηύδα used of Circe at 377.

sentences.t:
σοὶ μὲν νοστήσαντι, διοτρεφές, ὣς ἐχάρημεν,
ὡς εἴ τ’ εἰς Ἰθάκην ἀφικοίμεθα πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr:
soi men nostēsanti, diotrephes, hōs echarēmen,
hōs ei t’ eis Ithakēn aphikoimetha patrida gaian·
sentences.l:
‘For you, having come home, Zeus-nurtured one, we rejoiced so,
as if to Ithaca we had come, our fatherland;
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-nurtured one, we rejoiced at your return as much as if we had come to Ithaca, our fatherland;
sentences.n: The men speak; the Greek prints no quotation marks. σοὶ … νοστήσαντι is ‘at you having come home’: a dative with the aorist participle of νοστέω (νόστος ‘homecoming’). διοτρεφές is the vocative of διοτρεφής ‘nurtured by Zeus’, a title of kings and heroes. ὣς … ὡς εἰ is ‘so … as if’, and ἀφικοίμεθα is the optative ‘we had come’; τε after εἰ is the epic particle τε, which resists translation. ἐχάρημεν is the aorist passive of χαίρω ‘rejoice’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε, τῶν ἄλλων ἑτάρων κατάλεξον ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr: all’ age, tōn allōn hetarōn katalexon olethron.
sentences.l: but come, of the other companions recount the destruction.’
sentences.i: but come, recount the destruction of the rest of our companions.’
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’. τῶν ἄλλων ἑτάρων ‘of the other companions’ means the men who have not come back, and ὄλεθρον is ‘destruction’, the same word as in αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος. κατάλεξον is the aorist imperative of καταλέγω ‘tell in order, recount’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαν, αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ προσέφην μαλακοῖς ἐπέεσσι·
sentences.tr: hōs ephan, autar egō prosephēn malakois epeessi·
sentences.l: So they spoke, and I addressed them with soft words:
sentences.i: So they spoke, and I said to them in soft words:
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαν is ‘so they spoke’, the plural of ὣς ἔφατο (ἔφαν = ἔφασαν). προσέφην is a first-person past tense of πρόσφημι ‘address’, and μαλακοῖς ἐπέεσσι is ‘with soft words’, ἐπέεσσι being the epic dative plural of ἔπος. The raised point opens Odysseus' answer to the crew.

sentences.t:
νῆα μὲν ἂρ πάμπρωτον ἐρύσσομεν ἤπειρόνδε,
κτήματα δ’ ἐν σπήεσσι πελάσσομεν ὅπλα τε πάντα·
sentences.tr:
nēa men ar pamprōton eryssomen ēpeironde,
ktēmata d’ en spēessi pelassomen hopla te panta·
sentences.l:
‘The ship, then, first of all let us haul up onto land,
and the goods in caves let us bring near, and all the gear;
sentences.i: ‘First of all let us haul our ship up onto the land, and lay up our goods and all our tackle in caves;
sentences.n: Odysseus repeats Circe's instruction, with her plural imperatives (403–404) turned into ‘let us’. ἐρύσσομεν and πελάσσομεν are short-vowel subjunctives (= ἐρύσσωμεν, πελάσσωμεν) used as exhortations. The rest is as at 403–404: πάμπρωτον ‘first of all’, ἤπειρόνδε ‘to the land’, ὅπλα ‘gear’. What was Circe's command to him becomes his command to them.

sentences.t:
αὐτοὶ δ’ ὀτρύνεσθε ἐμοὶ ἅμα πάντες ἕπεσθαι,
ὄφρα ἴδηθ’ ἑτάρους ἱεροῖς ἐν δώμασι Κίρκης
πίνοντας καὶ ἔδοντας·
sentences.tr:
autoi d’ otrynesthe emoi hama pantes hepesthai,
ophra idēth’ hetarous hierois en dōmasi Kirkēs
pinontas kai edontas·
sentences.i: but you yourselves, all of you, rouse yourselves to follow along with me, so that you may see your companions drinking and eating in the sacred halls of Circe;
sentences.n: αὐτοί ‘you yourselves’ sets the men against the ship and the gear. ὀτρύνεσθε is the middle imperative of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, ‘bestir yourselves’, and ἐμοὶ ἅμα … ἕπεσθαι ‘to follow along with me’ has the infinitive of ἕπομαι. ὄφρα ἴδηθ’ is a purpose clause (ἴδητε, aorist subjunctive). ἱεροῖς … δώμασι ‘sacred halls’ is the adjective ἱερός ‘sacred’, as again at 445. The unit is cut at the raised point inside line 427.

sentences.t: ἐπηετανὸν γὰρ ἔχουσιν.
sentences.tr: epēetanon gar echousin.
sentences.l: for never-failing they have it.’
sentences.i: for they have a never-failing supply.’
sentences.n: ἐπηετανόν is of uncertain sense and is taken here as ‘never-failing, ample’; it is a neuter, used either as a noun, ‘a never-failing supply’, or as an adverb. γάρ gives the reason: Circe's hall is a place of plenty. ἔχουσιν is ‘they have’, with the food and drink of the line before in view.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, οἱ δ’ ὦκα ἐμοῖς ἐπέεσσι πίθοντο.
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, hoi d’ ōka emois epeessi pithonto.
sentences.l: So I spoke, and they quickly to my words were persuaded.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and they quickly yielded to my words.
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην ‘so I spoke’ closes Odysseus' speech. ὦκα is ‘quickly’, and ἐμοῖς ἐπέεσσι is the dative plural ‘to my words’. πίθοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of πείθομαι ‘be persuaded, obey’. The edition ends the sentence here with a full stop, and the narrative moves to the next event.

sentences.t: Εὐρύλοχος δέ μοι οἶος ἐρύκανε πάντας ἑταίρους·
sentences.tr: Eurylochos de moi oios erykane pantas hetairous·
sentences.l: And Eurylochus, to me, alone held back all my companions;
sentences.i: But Eurylochus alone was holding all my companions back;
sentences.n: Εὐρύλοχος is Eurylochus, a companion and, as line 441 shows, a relative of Odysseus. οἶος, with a smooth breathing, is ‘alone’. ἐρύκανε is a by-form of the imperfect of ἐρύκω ‘hold back, restrain’, so ‘was holding back’; μοι is a dative of interest, ‘on my side, of mine’, and πάντας ἑταίρους ‘all the companions’ is the object.

sentences.t: καί σφεας φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: kai spheas phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and having spoken to them, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and speaking up to them, he spoke winged words:
sentences.n: σφεας is the epic accusative plural ‘them’, and φωνήσας is the aorist participle of φωνέω ‘speak out’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula already met at 377. The edition ends the line with a raised point and the speech follows.

sentences.t: ἆ δειλοί, πόσ’ ἴμεν;
sentences.tr: a deiloi, pos’ imen;
sentences.l: ‘Oh, miserable ones, where are we going?
sentences.i: ‘Oh, you miserable men, where are we going?
sentences.n: Eurylochus speaks; the Greek prints no quotation marks. ἆ is an exclamation of reproach and pity, and δειλοί is the vocative plural of δειλός, ‘miserable’, not ‘cowardly’. πόσ’ is an elided adverb, ‘whither’, and ἴμεν is the short infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’ used for an indignant question: ‘where are we going?’. The unit is cut at the question mark.

sentences.t: τί κακῶν ἱμείρετε τούτων;
sentences.tr: ti kakōn himeirete toutōn;
sentences.l: Why of evils, of these, do you long?
sentences.i: Why do you long for these evils?
sentences.n: τί is ‘why?’, accusative as an adverb. ἱμείρετε is ‘you long for’ (ἱμείρω, from ἵμερος ‘longing’) and takes the genitive κακῶν τούτων ‘these evils’. The question has no object yet: what the men are longing to do comes in the next unit, as an infinitive in apposition.

sentences.t:
Κίρκης ἐς μέγαρον καταβήμεναι, ἥ κεν ἅπαντας
ἢ σῦς ἠὲ λύκους ποιήσεται ἠὲ λέοντας,
sentences.tr:
Kirkēs es megaron katabēmenai, hē ken hapantas
ē sys ēe lykous poiēsetai ēe leontas,
sentences.l:
Into Circe's hall to go down, who all of us
either swine or wolves will make, or lions,
sentences.i: To go down into Circe's hall, she who will make us all into swine or wolves or lions,
sentences.n: καταβήμεναι is the infinitive of καταβαίνω in the long ending -μεναι (= καταβῆναι); it stands in apposition to ‘these evils’. ἥ is the relative ‘she who’. κεν … ποιήσεται is ‘will make’ (middle, ‘make for herself’; the form may be a future or a short-vowel aorist subjunctive, = ποιήσηται); ἅπαντας is the object, and σῦς ‘swine’, λύκους ‘wolves’ and λέοντας ‘lions’ are the three things we are made into, joined by ἢ … ἠὲ … ἠὲ ‘either … or … or’. The unit stops at a comma because the sentence otherwise runs past four lines.

sentences.t:
οἵ κέν οἱ μέγα δῶμα φυλάσσοιμεν καὶ ἀνάγκῃ,
ὥς περ Κύκλωψ ἔρξ’, ὅτε οἱ μέσσαυλον ἵκοντο
ἡμέτεροι ἕταροι, σὺν δ’ ὁ θρασὺς εἵπετ’ Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr:
hoi ken hoi mega dōma phylassoimen kai anankēi,
hōs per Kyklōps erx’, hote hoi messaulon hikonto
hēmeteroi hetaroi, syn d’ ho thrasys heipet’ Odysseus·
sentences.i: we who would guard her great house, even under compulsion, as the Cyclops did when our companions came to his farmyard and bold Odysseus followed along with them;
sentences.n: οἵ is ‘we who’, the relative clause carrying on the object of ποιήσεται, with the optative φυλάσσοιμεν ‘we would guard’; οἱ is the enclitic dative ‘for her’, and ἀνάγκῃ is ‘by constraint’. ὥς περ Κύκλωψ ἔρξ’ is ‘just as the Cyclops did’: ἔρξ’ is ἔρξε, aorist of ἔρδω ‘do’, with the unexpressed object ‘this’. μέσσαυλον is the central enclosure of a steading, the yard in the middle. ἡμέτεροι ἕταροι is ‘our companions’ (ἕταροι = ἑταῖροι), σὺν … εἵπετ’ is tmesis, ‘followed along with them’ (ἕπομαι). θρασύς is ‘bold’; Eurylochus names Odysseus in the third person, and the epithet is not praise.

sentences.t: τούτου γὰρ καὶ κεῖνοι ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὄλοντο.
sentences.tr: toutou gar kai keinoi atasthaliēisin olonto.
sentences.l: for by this man's wanton-follies those men too perished.’
sentences.i: for through this man's wanton folly they too perished.’
sentences.n: τούτου ‘of this man’ is Odysseus, whom Eurylochus does not address, and κεῖνοι is ἐκεῖνοι ‘those men’. ἀτασθαλίῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν, and ὄλοντο the unaugmented aorist middle of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’. ἀτασθαλίαι is the word the proem uses at 1.7 for the companions' own fault, and here Eurylochus turns it against Odysseus. The accusation is the speaker's, and the translation keeps ‘wanton folly’ wherever the word stands.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε μετὰ φρεσὶ μερμήριξα,
σπασσάμενος τανύηκες ἄορ παχέος παρὰ μηροῦ,
τῷ οἱ ἀποπλήξας κεφαλὴν οὖδάσδε πελάσσαι,
καὶ πηῷ περ ἐόντι μάλα σχεδόν·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, autar egō ge meta phresi mermērixa,
spassamenos tanyēkes aor pacheos para mērou,
tōi hoi apoplēxas kephalēn oudasde pelassai,
kai pēōi per eonti mala schedon·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and I, for my part, in my mind pondered,
drawing the long-pointed sword from beside my stout thigh,
with it his head, having struck it off, to bring to the ground,
even though a kinsman-by-marriage he was, very close;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and I debated in my mind, drawing the long-pointed sword from beside my stout thigh, whether to strike off his head with it and bring it down to the ground, even though he was a relative by marriage, and a very close one;
sentences.n: μετὰ φρεσὶ μερμήριξα is ‘I pondered in my mind’, completed by the infinitive πελάσσαι (end of line 440): ‘whether to bring (his head) to the ground’. σπασσάμενος, the aorist middle participle of σπάω ‘draw’, shows the sword already out. τανύηκες is ‘long-pointed’ (τανυ- ‘long’ + ἀκ- ‘point’, as in πυριήκης; the second element is not fully certain), an adjective for ἄορ ‘sword’. τῷ is ‘with it’, οἱ ‘his’, ἀποπλήξας ‘having struck off’, and οὖδάσδε ‘to the ground’ (οὖδας with the suffix -δε). πηῷ ἐόντι, ‘being a relative by marriage’, agrees with οἱ: Eurylochus is Odysseus' kinsman. The unit is cut at the raised point inside line 441.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μ’ ἑταῖροι
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν ἐρήτυον ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος·
sentences.tr:
alla m’ hetairoi
meilichiois epeessin erētyon allothen allos·
sentences.l:
but my companions
with gentle words were restraining me, one from one side, one from another:
sentences.i: but my companions tried to hold me back with gentle words, one from one side and one from another:
sentences.n: μ’ is με ‘me’, the object of ἐρήτυον, the imperfect of ἐρητύω ‘hold back, restrain’, so ‘were trying to hold me back’. μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν is ‘with gentle words’, with the epic dative plural, and ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is ‘one from one place, another from another’ (-θεν ‘from’). The edition ends the line with a raised point, and the companions' words follow.

sentences.t:
διογενές, τοῦτον μὲν ἐάσομεν, εἰ σὺ κελεύεις,
αὐτοῦ πὰρ νηί τε μένειν καὶ νῆα ἔρυσθαι·
sentences.tr:
diogenes, touton men easomen, ei sy keleueis,
autou par nēi te menein kai nēa erysthai·
sentences.l:
‘Zeus-sprung one, this man, then, we will leave, if you bid it,
there by the ship to stay and the ship to guard;
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born one, we will leave this man, if you so bid, to stay right there by the ship and guard it;
sentences.n: The companions speak. διογενές is the vocative of διογενής ‘Zeus-born’. ἐάσομεν is ‘we will let, we will leave’ (ἐάω); τοῦτον μέν ‘this man’ is Eurylochus, set against ἡμῖν δέ ‘but for us’ in the next line. αὐτοῦ is ‘in that very place’, and πὰρ is παρά with its final vowel dropped (apocope, not elision). μένειν … ἔρυσθαι are infinitives depending on ἐάσομεν (‘let him stay and guard’): ἔρυσθαι is from ἐρύομαι ‘guard, protect’, a different verb from ἐρύω ‘haul’ in 403 and 423.

sentences.t: ἡμῖν δ’ ἡγεμόνευ’ ἱερὰ πρὸς δώματα Κίρκης.
sentences.tr: hēmin d’ hēgemoneu’ hiera pros dōmata Kirkēs.
sentences.l: and for us lead the way to the sacred halls of Circe.’
sentences.i: and lead us on to the sacred halls of Circe.’
sentences.n: ἡγεμόνευ’ is ἡγεμόνευε, the imperative of ἡγεμονεύω ‘lead the way’, and ἡμῖν ‘for us’ is the dative of those led. ἱερὰ … δώματα is ‘the sacred halls’, as at 426. πρός governs the accusative δώματα.

sentences.t: ὣς φάμενοι παρὰ νηὸς ἀνήιον ἠδὲ θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr: hōs phamenoi para nēos anēion ēde thalassēs.
sentences.l: So saying, from beside the ship and from the sea they went up.
sentences.i: So saying, they went up from the ship and the sea.
sentences.n: ὣς φάμενοι is ‘so saying’, the middle participle of φημί. ἀνήιον is the imperfect of ἄνειμι (ἀνά + εἶμι ‘go’), ‘went up’ inland, and παρὰ νηὸς ἠδὲ θαλάσσης is ‘from beside the ship and the sea’, the genitives with παρά meaning ‘from’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ μὲν Εὐρύλοχος κοίλῃ παρὰ νηὶ λέλειπτο,
ἀλλ’ ἕπετ’·
sentences.tr:
oude men Eurylochos koilēi para nēi leleipto,
all’ hepet’·
sentences.l:
Nor yet Eurylochus by the hollow ship was left behind,
but he followed;
sentences.i: Nor was Eurylochus left behind by the hollow ship; he followed;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ μέν is ‘nor yet’. λέλειπτο is the pluperfect passive of λείπω ‘had been left’, so ‘was left behind’, and κοίλῃ παρὰ νηί ‘beside the hollow ship’. ἕπετ’ is ἕπετο ‘he followed’ (ἕπομαι). The unit is cut at the raised point inside line 448.

sentences.t: ἔδεισεν γὰρ ἐμὴν ἔκπαγλον ἐνιπήν.
sentences.tr: edeisen gar emēn ekpaglon enipēn.
sentences.l: for he feared my terrifying rebuke.
sentences.i: for he feared my terrifying rebuke.
sentences.n: ἔδεισεν is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’, and γάρ gives the reason. ἔκπαγλος is built on ἐκπλήσσω ‘strike out of one's senses’, so ‘terrifying, astounding’. ἐνιπή is ‘rebuke’, here what Odysseus' reproach might be when he is angry; ἐμήν ‘my’ stands first and the whole phrase is the object.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δὲ τοὺς ἄλλους ἑτάρους ἐν δώμασι Κίρκη
ἐνδυκέως λοῦσέν τε καὶ ἔχρισεν λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρα χλαίνας οὔλας βάλεν ἠδὲ χιτῶνας·
sentences.tr:
tophra de tous allous hetarous en dōmasi Kirkē
endykeōs lousen te kai echrisen lip’ elaiōi,
amphi d’ ara chlainas oulas balen ēde chitōnas·
sentences.i: Meanwhile, in the halls, Circe kindly bathed the other companions and anointed them richly with oil, and threw thick cloaks and tunics about them;
sentences.n: τόφρα is ‘meanwhile’, and τοὺς ἄλλους ἑτάρους ‘the other companions’ are the men inside, who were not at the ship. ἐνδυκέως is ‘kindly’, λοῦσεν the aorist of λούω ‘wash, bathe’, and ἔχρισεν the aorist of χρίω ‘anoint’; λίπ’ is λίπα ‘richly’ (here with oil, ἐλαίῳ). ἀμφὶ … βάλεν is tmesis, ‘threw round’. χλαῖνα is a ‘cloak’, a man's heavy outer garment, and οὖλος is ‘thick, woolly’; χιτών is the tunic worn under it.

sentences.t: δαινυμένους δ’ ἐὺ πάντας ἐφεύρομεν ἐν μεγάροισιν.
sentences.tr: dainymenous d’ ey pantas epheuromen en megaroisin.
sentences.l: and feasting well, all of them, we found in the halls.
sentences.i: and we found them all feasting well in the halls.
sentences.n: δαινυμένους is ‘feasting’ (δαίνυμαι) and ἐὺ ‘well’ is an adverb. ἐφεύρομεν is the aorist of ἐφευρίσκω ‘find’ in the first person plural: Odysseus and the men who followed him. μεγάροισιν is the epic dative plural of μέγαρον ‘hall’, plural for the one house.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ ἀλλήλους εἶδον φράσσαντό τ’ ἐσάντα,
κλαῖον ὀδυρόμενοι, περὶ δὲ στεναχίζετο δῶμα.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei allēlous eidon phrassanto t’ esanta,
klaion odyromenoi, peri de stenachizeto dōma.
sentences.l:
And they, when one another they saw and took note of face to face,
wept, lamenting, and around groaned the house.
sentences.i: And when they saw one another and took in the sight face to face, they wept and lamented, and the whole house resounded with their groans.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ ‘they’ are the restored men now meeting those from the ship. ἀλλήλους is ‘one another’, εἶδον the aorist of ὁράω (with its augment; ἴδον at 414 has none), and φράσσαντο the aorist middle of φράζομαι ‘notice, take note’; ἐσάντα is ‘opposite, face to face’. κλαῖον ὀδυρόμενοι is ‘wept, lamenting’. περὶ … στεναχίζετο is tmesis: the middle of στεναχίζω ‘groan’, ‘the house groaned all round’, the house taking up the sound.

sentences.t: ἡ δέ μευ ἄγχι στᾶσα προσηύδα δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: hē de meu anchi stasa prosēuda dia theaōn·
sentences.l: And she, close to me having stood, spoke to me, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: And she, heavenly even among goddesses, came and stood close beside me and spoke:
sentences.n: The line is the same as 400 and takes the same English. μευ is the genitive ‘me’ with ἄγχι ‘near’, στᾶσα ‘having stood’, and δῖα θεάων ‘heavenly among goddesses’; her second speech follows in the next unit. Murray's numbering passes from 455 to 457: this edition prints no line 456, and the next unit begins at 457.

sentences.t: μηκέτι νῦν θαλερὸν γόον ὄρνυτε·
sentences.tr: mēketi nyn thaleron goon ornyte·
sentences.l: ‘No longer now an abundant lament rouse up;
sentences.i: ‘Now rouse your abundant lament no more;
sentences.n: Circe speaks; the Greek prints no quotation marks. μηκέτι ‘no longer’ with the present imperative ὄρνυτε (ὄρνυμι ‘rouse, stir up’) is a prohibition: ‘stop raising’. γόον is ‘lament’, and θαλερόν ‘blooming, luxuriant’ is the same word used of the tears at 409: full, copious. The unit is cut at the raised point inside line 457. The numbering follows Murray: this unit begins at 457, with no line 456 between it and 455.

sentences.t:
οἶδα καὶ αὐτὴ
ἠμὲν ὅσ’ ἐν πόντῳ πάθετ’ ἄλγεα ἰχθυόεντι,
ἠδ’ ὅσ’ ἀνάρσιοι ἄνδρες ἐδηλήσαντ’ ἐπὶ χέρσου.
sentences.tr:
oida kai autē
ēmen hos’ en pontōi pathet’ algea ichthyoenti,
ēd’ hos’ anarsioi andres edēlēsant’ epi chersou.
sentences.l:
I know it myself,
both what pains you suffered on the fish-teeming open-sea,
and what hostile men did to harm you on dry land.
sentences.i: I know it myself, both all the pains you suffered on the fish-teeming sea and all the harm hostile men did you on dry land.
sentences.n: οἶδα is ‘I know’, and καὶ αὐτή ‘I myself’. ἠμὲν … ἠδ’ is ‘both … and’. ὅσ’ … ἄλγεα is ‘all the pains’ and πάθετ’ the second person plural aorist of πάσχω, unaugmented. ἰχθυόεντι ‘fish-teeming’ is ἰχθύς ‘fish’ with the suffix -όεις ‘full of’. ἀνάρσιοι is ‘hostile’, and ἐδηλήσαντο the aorist middle of δηλέομαι ‘harm, injure’, with ὅσ’ ‘all that harm’ as its object; χέρσου is the genitive of χέρσος ‘dry land’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ ἐσθίετε βρώμην καὶ πίνετε οἶνον,
εἰς ὅ κεν αὖτις θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι λάβητε,
οἷον ὅτε πρώτιστον ἐλείπετε πατρίδα γαῖαν
τρηχείης Ἰθάκης.
sentences.tr:
all’ aget’ esthiete brōmēn kai pinete oinon,
eis ho ken autis thymon eni stēthessi labēte,
hoion hote prōtiston eleipete patrida gaian
trēcheiēs Ithakēs.
sentences.l:
But come, eat food and drink wine,
until again heart in your breasts you take,
such as when first you left your fatherland,
of rough Ithaca.
sentences.i: But come, eat food and drink wine, until you have again in your breasts the heart you had when you first left your fatherland, rough Ithaca.
sentences.n: ἐσθίετε and πίνετε are present imperatives, ‘eat’ and ‘drink’; βρώμην is ‘food’. εἰς ὅ κεν … λάβητε is ‘until you take’, with the aorist subjunctive. θυμὸν … λάβητε is ‘take heart’, with θυμός in its sense of the heart as the seat of courage and feeling, and οἷον ὅτε … is ‘such (a heart) as when’. ἐλείπετε is the imperfect ‘you were leaving’, and πατρίδα γαῖαν τρηχείης Ἰθάκης ‘your fatherland, rough Ithaca’ closes the unit at the full stop inside line 463.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἀσκελέες καὶ ἄθυμοι,
αἰὲν ἄλης χαλεπῆς μεμνημένοι, οὐδέ ποθ’ ὕμιν
θυμὸς ἐν εὐφροσύνῃ, ἐπεὶ ἦ μάλα πολλὰ πέποσθε.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ askelees kai athymoi,
aien alēs chalepēs memnēmenoi, oude poth’ hymin
thymos en euphrosynēi, epei ē mala polla peposthe.
sentences.l:
But now you are withered and without-heart,
always of the harsh wandering mindful, and never for you
the heart in cheer, since in truth very many things you have suffered.’
sentences.i: But now you are withered and disheartened, always remembering your harsh wandering, and your heart is never in good cheer, since you have truly suffered so much.’
sentences.n: ἀσκελέες is ‘withered, dried up’, apparently from σκέλλω ‘dry up’, here of the body drained of its life; ἄθυμοι is ‘without heart’ (ἀ- + θυμός). αἰέν is αἰεί ‘always’, and μεμνημένοι the perfect middle participle of μιμνῄσκομαι ‘remember’, with the genitive ἄλης χαλεπῆς ‘harsh wandering’. ὕμιν is the dative ὑμῖν ‘for you’, so ‘never is your heart in cheer’. ἦ μάλα πολλὰ πέποσθε is ‘truly you have suffered very much’, πέποσθε being the epic second person perfect of πάσχω.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἡμῖν δ’ αὖτ’ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hēmin d’ aut’ epepeitheto thymos agēnōr.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and then our own lordly heart was persuaded;
sentences.i: So she said, and our own proud hearts were won over.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so she spoke’, the τ written θ before the rough breathing of ἡμῖν. ἡμῖν δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘and to us in turn’: the men's turn to yield, as Odysseus' own heart yielded at 406 (the English of this line is kept as shipped, which takes ἡμῖν as ‘our own’ and αὖτ’ as ‘then’). ἐπεπείθετο is the imperfect middle of πείθω ‘be persuaded, obey’, with the dative ‘to us’. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is the phrase of 406, where the house rendering ‘manly spirit’ / ‘proud spirit’ stands; the shipped English of this line says ‘lordly heart’ / ‘proud hearts’, left as shipped.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν ἤματα πάντα τελεσφόρον εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν
ἥμεθα δαινύμενοι κρέα τ’ ἄσπετα καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ·
sentences.tr:
entha men ēmata panta telesphoron eis eniauton
hēmetha dainymenoi krea t’ aspeta kai methy hēdy·
sentences.l:
There all the days, for a completion-bearing year,
we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.i: There, for a full year, on every day, we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.n: ἤματα πάντα is ‘all the days’, and τελεσφόρον εἰς ἐνιαυτόν is ‘for a year that brings its completion’, a year taken to its full (τέλος ‘end’ + φέρω ‘bear’). ἥμεθα is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and δαινύμενοι ‘feasting’. Line 468 is identical to 9.162, and the English of that line is kept. κρέα ἄσπετα is ‘boundless meat’, and μέθυ ἡδύ ‘sweet wine’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἐνιαυτὸς ἔην, περὶ δ’ ἔτραπον ὧραι
μηνῶν φθινόντων, περὶ δ’ ἤματα μακρὰ τελέσθη,
καὶ τότε μ’ ἐκκαλέσαντες ἔφαν ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ eniautos eēn, peri d’ etrapon hōrai
mēnōn phthinontōn, peri d’ ēmata makra telesthē,
kai tote m’ ekkalesantes ephan eriēres hetairoi·
sentences.l:
but when at last a year was, and the seasons turned round,
the months waning, and the long days were fulfilled round,
then me, calling me out, said my trusty companions:
sentences.i: but when at last a year had come, and the seasons had turned as the months waned, and the long days had run their course, then my trusty companions called me out and said:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ῥ’ is ‘but when at last’. ἐνιαυτὸς ἔην is ‘a year was’ (ἔην = ἦν); περὶ … ἔτραπον is tmesis, ‘turned round’, of the ὧραι ‘seasons’, and μηνῶν φθινόντων is the genitive absolute ‘the months waning’. περὶ … τελέσθη is tmesis again: τελέσθη is the aorist passive of τελέω ‘bring to an end’, with a neuter plural subject ἤματα μακρά ‘the long days’. ἐκκαλέσαντες is ‘having called out’, and ἔφαν the plural of ἔφη ‘said’. The raised point opens the crew's speech.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνι’, ἤδη νῦν μιμνήσκεο πατρίδος αἴης,
εἴ τοι θέσφατόν ἐστι σαωθῆναι καὶ ἱκέσθαι
οἶκον ἐς ὑψόροφον καὶ σὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
daimoni’, ēdē nyn mimnēskeo patridos aiēs,
ei toi thesphaton esti saōthēnai kai hikesthai
oikon es hypsorophon kai sēn es patrida gaian.
sentences.l:
‘Strange man, already now be mindful of your fatherland,
if for you it is god-declared to be saved and to reach
your high-roofed home and your own fatherland.’
sentences.i: ‘Strange man, now at last think of your fatherland, if it is decreed for you to be saved and to reach your high-roofed home and your own native land.’
sentences.n: The crew speak; the Greek prints no quotation marks. δαιμόνιε, from δαίμων ‘divine power’, is an address of uncertain force: ‘strange one, man driven by something beyond himself’, whether gentle reproach or plain urging is not known. μιμνήσκεο is the uncontracted imperative of μιμνῄσκομαι ‘remember’, with the genitive πατρίδος αἴης ‘fatherland’. θέσφατόν ἐστι is ‘it is god-declared, decreed’, with the infinitives σαωθῆναι ‘to be saved’ and ἱκέσθαι ‘to reach’. οἶκον ἐς ὑψόροφον is ‘to the high-roofed house’. Line 474 already stands in a published unit and its English is kept, including ‘native land’ where this part otherwise says ‘fatherland’. The speech and the part end together.
